rows.speaker: many
rows.claim: Many understand the victory as the conquest of Makkah, extending to future Muslim victories.
rows.anchor: understood by many as a reference to the conquest of Makkah

rows.speaker: many of the Prophet’s Companions
rows.claim: Companions including Ibn Masʿūd and Anas ibn Mālik understood the victory specifically as the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah.
rows.anchor: many of the Prophet’s Companions, such as Ibn Masʿūd and Anas ibn Mālik, saw it as a specific reference to the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Treaty opened contact between Muslims and non-Muslims, increasing Islam’s adherents and explaining its status as a victory.
rows.anchor: as this treaty allowed Muslims and non-Muslims to mix more freely and thus resulted in an increase in the number of adherents to Islam

rows.speaker: Ibn Masʿūd
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd contrasted others’ celebration of Makkah’s conquest with his view that Ḥudaybiyah was the victory.
rows.anchor: Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said, “You consider the conquering of Makkah to be the victory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may refer to Islam’s victory through proofs and revelation.
rows.anchor: The verse can also be understood as a reference to the victory of Islam by means of proofs and revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatḥ means both victory and opening.
rows.anchor: Victory translates fatḥ, which also means “opening.”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read fatḥ as the heart’s opening and the unveiling of the Divine Essence, Attributes, and Acts.
rows.anchor: some understand fatḥ as a reference to the opening of the heart

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators understand the promise as forgiveness for all the Prophet’s past and future sins.
rows.anchor: Many commentators understand v. 2 to mean that God has forgiven the Prophet all of his sins, past and future

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators use this promise as proof of the Prophet’s spiritual inerrancy (ʿiṣmah).
rows.anchor: thus some take it as a proof-text for the spiritual inerrancy

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One reading places the sins before and after the manifest victory.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, thy sins that went before refers to sins committed before the manifest victory

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another reading refers to the periods before and after revelation began.
rows.anchor: Others say this verse refers to the period before and the period after the revelation began

rows.speaker: still others
rows.claim: A further reading means what preceded this verse’s revelation and what followed it.
rows.anchor: while still others say it means what preceded the revelation of this verse and what followed it

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Despite the promise, the Prophet continued night prayer until his feet swelled while seeking God’s forgiveness.
rows.anchor: the Prophet continued to stand in prayer at night until his feet swelled

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Asked why he prayed, the Prophet answered that he should be a thankful servant.
rows.anchor: When asked why he did so, the Prophet replied, “Should I not be a thankful servant?”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completing God’s blessing is explained as attaining Paradise, receiving prophethood and wisdom, or gaining the conquests of Khaybar, Makkah, and Ṭāʾif.
rows.anchor: Complete His Blessing refers to attaining Paradise, the blessing of prophethood and wisdom, or the conquests of Khaybar, Makkah, and Ṭāʾif

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The judgment is linked to 52:7; wāqiʿ may mean “shall befall,” with a parallel note at 56:1–2.
rows.anchor: Cf. 52:7. Shall come to pass can also be translated shall befall

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Najm is usually dated to early Makkah, soon after Sūrah 112, al-Ikhlāṣ.
rows.anchor: usually considered an early Makkan sūrah, revealed soon after Sūrah 112, al-Ikhlāṣ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 13–18 refer to the Ascension and may belong to a later period than the early Makkan setting.
rows.anchor: Vv. 13–18, which refer to the Ascension of the Prophet, may, however, be from a later period

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators date the Ascension to the late Makkan period, most likely 619.
rows.anchor:
many commentators maintain that the Ascension of the Prophet Muhammad (miʿrāj
) did not occur until the late Makkan period, most likely in the year 619

rows.speaker: a minority
rows.claim: A minority dates the Ascension to 614, seven years before the hijrah.
rows.anchor: a minority maintain that it occurred seven years before the hijrah in 614

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some consider verse 32 to be from the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: V. 32 is also considered by some to be from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some extend the proposed Madinan dating to verse 33.
rows.anchor: to which some add v. 33

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the star oath with which it begins.
rows.anchor: Al-Najm takes its name from the oath with which it opens, By the star

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tradition reports this as the first sūrah the Prophet recited publicly in Makkah.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is reported to be the first that the Prophet recited in public in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The star reference links back to the injunction in 52:49 to glorify God as the stars recede.
rows.anchor: the injunction in 52:49 to glorify God at the receding of the stars

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening responds to the disbelievers’ claim in 52:33 that the Prophet invented the revelation.
rows.anchor: the opening verses respond to the contention of the disbelievers in 52:33, He has invented it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is famous for its rhetorical power and the dispute over the meaning of its opening section.
rows.anchor: because of its poetic rhetorical power and the debate that arises

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators identify the passage as the Prophet’s two visions of Gabriel in his true form, unlike Gabriel’s usual human appearance.
rows.anchor: Many commentators say the passage refers to the Prophet’s two visions of the Archangel Gabriel in his true form

rows.speaker: many others
rows.claim: Many others read the passage as the Prophet seeing God, by heart alone or by both eye and heart, during the Night Journey and Ascension.
rows.anchor: Many others interpret it as a reference to the Prophet’s vision of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second section reproaches Quraysh for idol worship, discusses its roots in ignorance and conjecture, and condemns seeking angels’ intercession.
rows.anchor: The second section (vv. 19–30) reproaches the Quraysh for worshipping idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 31 contrasts punishment for evildoers with reward for the virtuous before the next section.
rows.anchor: After contrasting the punishment of those who do evil with the rewards of those who are virtuous (v. 31)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third section calls people to reflect on their creation and transitions to enduring truths in the scriptures of Moses and Abraham.
rows.anchor: the third section (vv. 31–54) calls upon people to reflect upon their creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This section then turns to perennial truths attested in the scriptures of Moses and Abraham.
rows.anchor: transitions into a discussion of the perennial truths attested in the scriptures of Moses and Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah briefly recalls the destruction of earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: This is followed by a brief reference to the destruction of former peoples

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section admonishes listeners to heed the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: a final admonition to heed the Quran

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say al-Lāt is shortened from al-Ilāhah, meaning “the Goddess.”
rows.anchor: Al-Lāt (which some say is a shortened form al-Ilāhah, meaning “the Goddess”) is said to have been a white stone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Lāt was said to be an inscribed white stone at Ṭāʾif, near Makkah.
rows.anchor: a white stone with inscriptions in the city of Ṭāʾif, the sister city of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tribe of Thaqīf worshipped al-Lāt.
rows.anchor: that was worshipped by the tribe of Thaqīf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿUzzā means “the Most Mighty,” refers to Venus or the morning star, and was worshipped by Ghaṭfān.
rows.anchor: Al-ʿUzzā (meaning “the Most Mighty” and referring to Venus or the morning star), worshipped by the tribe of Ghaṭfān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿUzzā’s shrine at Nakhlah consisted of three trees, a monument, and curtains.
rows.anchor: had a shrine consisting of three trees on which the idolaters placed a monument and curtains in the area of Nakhlah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿUzzā is said to have been Quraysh’s most venerated idol.
rows.anchor: she is said to have been the most venerated idol among the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manāt was worshipped by Khuzaʿah, Aws, and Khazraj and was regarded as the goddess of destiny.
rows.anchor: Manāt, worshipped by the tribes of Khuzaʿah, Aws, and Khazraj, was said to be the goddess of destiny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manāt’s shrine was at Mushallal near Qudayd, between Makkah and Madinah.
rows.anchor: her shrine was in the area of Mushallal near Qudayd, between Makkah and Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Together al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt formed a triad.
rows.anchor: The three idols together formed a triad.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three were sometimes said to be daughters of “Allāh,” a belief alluded to in verses 21–22.
rows.anchor: Sometimes all three were said to be daughters of “Allāh,” an idea alluded to in vv. 21–22

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some accounts instead made al-Lāt and Manāt daughters of al-ʿUzzā.
rows.anchor: sometimes al-Lāt and Manāt were considered daughters of al-ʿUzzā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many other idols were worshipped in Arabia, but these three are singled out for fame or proximity to Makkah.
rows.anchor: these three are mentioned because they were more famous (IK) or because of their proximity to Makkah

rows.speaker: early histories of Islam
rows.claim: Early Islamic histories report that Satan whispered two fabricated verses to the Prophet after his recitation of 53:19–20, elevating the idols.
rows.anchor: In several early histories of Islam, it is reported that when the Prophet came to the end of vv. 19–20 Satan whispered to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged lines called the idols high-flying cranes and said their intercession was hoped for.
rows.anchor: “Verily, they are high flying cranes! And their intercession is indeed anticipated/hoped for.”

rows.speaker: some accounts
rows.claim: The verses pleased Quraysh; some accounts say they prostrated with the Prophet and his followers at verse 62.
rows.anchor: who according to some accounts then prostrated with the Prophet and his followers when the Prophet reached v. 62

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The incident briefly eased Muslim persecution.
rows.anchor: As a result, the persecution of Muslims abated for a brief period.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet later recognized the deception upon revelation of 22:52, recanted the interpolation, and Quraysh persecution resumed.
rows.anchor: The Prophet later realized that he had been deceived when he received the revelation of 22:52

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tradition calls the story the “Story of the Cranes,” while modern Western literature calls it the “Satanic Verses.”
rows.anchor: This is known as the “Story of the Cranes” in the Islamic tradition and as the“Satanic Verses” in modern Western literature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the idols names means they exist only in imagination, as Joseph says of such worship in 12:40.
rows.anchor: as in the Prophet Joseph’s words to his fellow prisoners in 12:40: You worship apart from Him naught but names that you have named

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conjecture is what one follows without knowledge, with a parallel discussion at 53:28.
rows.anchor: Conjecture is what one follows in the absence of knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That which their souls desire” refers to caprice, which wanders from one direction to another in the absence of truth.
rows.anchor: while that which their souls desire refers to their caprice, which is the tendency to wander one way and then another in the absence of truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may be rendered more literally as “that which their souls fancy.”
rows.anchor: The phrase could also be translated more literally, “that which their souls fancy.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following desire or fancy means yielding to the soul that commands evil, as discussed in 12:53.
rows.anchor: To follow that which their souls desire or “fancy” is to succumb to the soul that commands to evil
